lesson.title: The Full Nodal Analysis Toolkit: Nodes and Supernodes Together
lesson.summary: Nodal analysis is the systematic combination of the node voltage method with supernodes, classifying every node in a real circuit and writing exactly as many equations as unknowns.
lesson.body:
The node voltage method and the supernode technique are really two halves of one complete procedure, and putting them together into a single systematic workflow is what nodal analysis means in practice. Real circuits rarely offer the luxury of only ordinary nodes or only supernodes, most nontrivial circuits need both at once: some voltage sources are conveniently tied to the reference node, effectively fixing a node voltage directly and removing an unknown entirely, others float between two non-reference nodes and require the supernode treatment, and everything else gets an ordinary KCL equation.

The systematic approach is to first identify the reference node and label it 0 volts, then scan every remaining node and classify it: if a node is directly set by a voltage source to the reference, its value is already known, no equation needed. If two nodes are joined by a floating voltage source, group them into a supernode, write one KCL equation for the combined boundary, and one constraint equation from the source. Every other node gets an ordinary KCL equation in terms of the unknown node voltages. The result is always exactly as many independent equations as unknowns, solvable as a linear system.

Consider a three node circuit beyond the reference. A 6 amp current source injects into node 1. A 3 ohm resistor connects node 1 to ground, and a 2 ohm resistor connects node 1 to node 2. Node 2 and node 3 form a supernode, joined by a 4 volt source with the plus terminal at node 2. An 8 ohm resistor connects node 2 to ground, and a 4 ohm resistor connects node 3 to ground. The node 1 equation is 6 equals V1 over 3, plus (V1 minus V2) over 2. The supernode equation, current in from node 1 equals current out to ground through both resistors, is (V1 minus V2) over 2 equals V2 over 8, plus V3 over 4. The constraint is V2 minus V3 equals 4.

Solving this system gives V1 equals 12 volts, V2 equals 8 volts, and V3 equals 4 volts. Checking node 1: 12 over 3 is 4 amps, plus (12 minus 8) over 2, which is 2 amps, totals 6 amps, matching the source. Checking the supernode: (12 minus 8) over 2 is 2 amps in, and 8 over 8, plus 4 over 4, is 1 plus 1, or 2 amps out, balanced exactly. Checking the constraint: 8 minus 4 is 4 volts, matching the source.

This three step habit, classify every node, write the minimum necessary equations, then verify every equation independently once numbers are in hand, is what separates reliable nodal analysis from error prone guesswork, especially as circuits grow past three or four nodes where mental arithmetic alone stops being trustworthy. It is also worth noting that a supernode is not limited to exactly two nodes: if a chain of floating voltage sources links three or more non-reference nodes together, all of them merge into one larger supernode, with one KCL equation for the entire combined boundary and one constraint equation for every source inside it, the same bookkeeping just extended to a bigger group.
